rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tabari defines praise as pure thanks to God alone for countless gifts, including faculties for obedience, worldly provision without entitlement, and guidance to lasting bliss; all praise belongs to Him at first and last.
rows.anchor: الشكر خالصا لله جل ثناؤه دون سائر ما يُعْبَد من دونه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas says Gabriel instructed Muhammad to say “praise be to God”; he glosses it as thanks, submission, and acknowledgment of God's blessing and guidance.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس :  الحمد لله :  هو الشكر

rows.speaker: الحكم بن عمير
rows.claim: Al-Hakam ibn ʿUmayr reports the Prophet's statement that saying “praise be to God, Lord of the worlds” is gratitude to God and brings an increase.
rows.anchor: عن الحكم بن عمير وكانت له صحبة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: An unnamed view distinguishes praise of God through His beautiful names and attributes from thanks for His favors and gifts.
rows.anchor: وقد قيل إن قول القائل

rows.speaker: كعب الأحبار
rows.claim: Kaʿb al-Aḥbār reports that whoever says “praise be to God” has praised God.
rows.anchor: عن كعب قال :  من قال :  «الحمد لله » فذلك ثناء على الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tabari notes that Kaʿb's report does not clarify whether praise means praise through God's names and attributes or praise for His blessings.
rows.anchor: ولم يبين في الرواية عنه من أي معنيي الثناء اللذين ذكرنا ذلك

rows.speaker: النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم
rows.claim: The Prophet says nothing is more beloved to God than praise, and that God praised Himself by saying “praise be to God.”
rows.anchor: عن الأسود بن سريع ،  أن النبيّ صلى الله عليه وسلم قال :  «ليس شيء أحبّ إليه الحمد من الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tabari argues that Arabic usage allows praise and thanks to stand for one another, since speakers can say “praise be to God, as thanks.”
rows.anchor: من الحكم لقول القائل :  الحَمْدُ لِلّهِ شكرا بالصحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The definite article in al-ḥamd signals all praise and complete thanks belong to God; without it, the phrase would denote only this speaker's praise.
rows.anchor: جميع المحامد والشكر الكامل لله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Readers and scholars unanimously vocalize al-ḥamdu in the nominative; al-Tabari says the accusative would distort the meaning and merits punishment if knowingly read.
rows.anchor: قراءة القراءة وعلماء الأمة على رفع الحمد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God speaks both clauses: He praises Himself, then teaches and obliges His servants to recite them as a test, with an understood command to say them signaled by “You alone we worship.”
rows.anchor: بل ذلك كله كلام الله جل ثناؤه ولكنه جل ذكره حمد نفسه وأثنى عليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command “say” is omitted because Arabic speakers omit words recoverable from context; here the following worship clause reveals that the praise clause is also an instruction to servants.
rows.anchor: أغنت دلالة ما ظهر عليه من القول عن إبداء ما حذف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For rab as obedient master or chief, al-Tabari cites Labīd's “lord of Kinda” and al-Nābigha's “lord of my possessions.”
rows.anchor: وأهْلَكْنَ يَوْما رَبّ كِنْدَةَ وابنَه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rab can mean one who repairs or tends something: al-Farazdaq calls an unrepaired hide “not tended,” while ʿAlqama describes another king tending his affairs.
rows.anchor: يعني بذلك في أديم غير مصلح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third Arabic sense is owner: one who possesses a thing is called its rabb.
rows.anchor: والمالك للشيء يدعى ربه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God is the incomparable master, the one who sets His creatures' affairs right through His gifts, and the owner of creation and command.
rows.anchor: والمصلح أمر خلقه بما أسبغ عليهم من نعمه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas glosses “Lord of the worlds” as the one who owns all creation, the heavens, earth, their inhabitants, and all between them, known and unknown; nothing resembles Him.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس :  يقول قل الحمد لله الذي له الخلق كله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ʿālamūn is the plural of ʿālam, while ʿālam is a collective noun with no singular form from the same word, like anām, rahṭ, and jaysh.
rows.anchor: لا واحد له من لفظه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ʿālam names classes of peoples and each generation in its era; humans, jinn, and every other created kind form worlds. Al-ʿAjjāj's poem uses “this world” for his contemporaries.
rows.anchor: قول العجاج :  *** *** فخندف هامة هذا العالمِ

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report through ʿIkrima attributes to Ibn ʿAbbas the view that the worlds are jinn and humans.
rows.anchor: عن عكرمة ،  عن ابن عباس :  رب العالمين :  الجن والإنس

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A report through Saʿīd ibn Jubayr also attributes to Ibn ʿAbbas the gloss “Lord of the jinn and humans.”
rows.anchor: عن سعيد بن جبير ،  عن ابن عباس ،  في قول الله جل وعزّ :  رب العالمين :  قال :  رب الجن والإنس

rows.speaker: سعيد بن جبير
rows.claim: Saʿīd ibn Jubayr says Adam's descendants, jinn, and humans each constitute a distinct world.
rows.anchor: عن سعيد بن جبير ،  قوله :  رب العالمين قال :  ابن آدم ،  والجن والإنس كل أمة منهم عالم على حِدَته

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujāhid interprets “Lord of the worlds” as Lord of humans and jinn.
rows.anchor: عن مجاهد :  الحمد لله رب العالمين قال :  الإنس والجنّ

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: Qatāda says every kind is a world.
rows.anchor: عن قتادة :  رب العالمين قال :  كل صنف :  عالم

rows.speaker: أبو العالية
rows.claim: Abū al-ʿĀliya says humans and jinn are worlds, alongside either eighteen thousand or fourteen thousand other worlds (he is unsure), of angels on earth, 3,500 in each corner, created to worship God.
rows.anchor: عن أبي العالية ،   في قوله

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj interprets the worlds as jinn and humans.
rows.anchor: عن ابن جريج ،  في قوله :  رب العالمين قال :  الجن والإنس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tabari interprets “You alone we worship” as humbling, abasing, and submitting ourselves to God alone, acknowledging His lordship.
rows.anchor: لك اللهم نخشع ،  ونذلّ ،  ونستكين ،  إقرارا لك يا ربنا بالربوبية لا لغيرك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas reports Gabriel's gloss that worship means to affirm God's oneness, fear Him, and hope in Him alone.
rows.anchor: عن عبد الله بن عباس ،  قال :  قال جبريل لمحمد صلى الله عليه وسلم :  قل يا محمد :  إياك نعبد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tabari prefers humility and submission to fear and hope because worship in Arabic fundamentally means abasement; the road called muʿabbad is trodden and subdued, as in Ṭarafa's verse, and a ridden camel is also muʿabbad.
rows.anchor: قول طَرَفة بن العبد :  تُبَارِي عِتَاقا ناجياتٍ وأتْبَعَتْ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The servants seek God's aid for worship, obedience, and all their affairs, relying on no one else, unlike disbelievers who seek aid from the idols they worship.
rows.anchor: وإياك ربنا نستعين على عبادتنا إياك وطاعتنا لك وفي أمورنا كلها لا أحد سواك

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas glosses the request as seeking God's aid for obedience and all one's affairs.
rows.anchor: عن عبد الله بن عباس :  وإياك نستعين قال :  إياك :  نستعين على طاعتك وعلى أمورنا كلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The believer asks for help with obedience during the remaining life, not past deeds; God's enabling of the limbs and gift of guidance are grace, not an obligation, and granting or withholding aid entails neither injustice nor faulty governance.
rows.anchor: داعٍ أن يعينه فيما بقي من عمره على ما كلفه من طاعته ،  دون ما قد تَقَضّى ومضى

rows.speaker: القائلين بالتفويض من أهل القدر
rows.claim: Al-Tabari rejects the Qadari delegation claim that God may command a duty only after making its performance and omission possible through necessary aid; the verse teaches believers to ask for assistance as a divine favor.
rows.anchor: أدل الدليل على فساد قول القائلين بالتفويض من أهل القدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He argues that the Qadari premise makes asking for aid equivalent to asking God not to act unjustly, but Muslims approve the former supplication and reject the latter, exposing the premise's error.
rows.anchor: وفي إجماع أهل الإسلام جميعا على تصويب قول القائل :  اللهم إنا نستعينك وتخطئتهم قول القائل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Worship precedes the request for aid because each entails the other: a servant cannot worship without God's aid, and aid for worship is realized in the servant's act; either order conveys the relation.
rows.anchor: كان سواء تقديم ما قدم منهما على صاحبه ،  كما سواء قولك للرجل إذا قضى حاجتك فأحسن إليك

rows.speaker: بعض أهل الغفلة
rows.claim: Some inattentive readers took the verse as an instance of fronting and delaying the intended order, like Imruʾ al-Qays's line about enough money and seeking more.
rows.anchor: وقد ظن بعض أهل الغفلة أن ذلك من المقدم الذي معناه التأخير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tabari rejects the delayed-order analogy: having enough money does not prevent seeking more, whereas worship and divine aid entail one another, so their stated order is sound.
rows.anchor: ومن مشابهة بيت امرىء القيس بمعزلٍ من أجل أنه قد يكفيه القليل من المال ويطلب الكثير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fronted object pronoun is repeated with each verb because each verb governs its own object; Arabic speech is more eloquent when the object is repeated, though omission is permissible when the pronoun follows the verb.
rows.anchor: كان الأفصح إعادتها مع كل فعل .  كما كان الفصيح من الكلام إعادتها مع كل فعل

rows.speaker: بعض من لم يمعن النظر
rows.claim: Some who did not examine closely compared the repeated “You alone” to the repeated “between” in verses by ʿAdī ibn Zayd and al-Aʿshā of Hamdān.
rows.anchor: ظن بعض من لم يمعن النظر أن إعادة «إياك » مع «نستعين » بعد تقدمها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tabari rejects the analogy: “between” requires two complements and is incomplete when one is omitted, but “You alone we worship” is already a complete clause, and each verb properly takes the repeated object.
rows.anchor: حاجة كل كلمة كانت نظيرة «إياك نعبد » إلى «إياك » كحاجة «نعبد » إليها
